questions.prompt: A therapist says, “Appearance is only about looking attractive in the uniform.” What is the most accurate response?
options: That is correct. Attractiveness is the whole standard.
The Appearance Standard is about cleanliness, neatness, freshness, professionalism, confidence, and readiness to serve — not simply looking attractive.
Appearance only matters if management is watching.
Massage skill makes appearance unimportant.

questions.prompt: Why is professional appearance part of the massage service itself?
options: Because clients never notice hygiene during close contact.
Because massage involves close physical contact, so the client will notice uniform, hair, hands, nails, breath, body odour, footwear, and overall presentation.
Because appearance is only for photos.
Because therapists represent themselves, not Zura Spa.

questions.prompt: A therapist thinks, “This is only about how I personally look.” What may the client think instead?
options: “This is how Zura Spa operates.” One therapist’s appearance can strengthen or weaken the whole brand.
“This has nothing to do with the spa.”
“I will only judge the oil.”
“Appearance is optional if the massage is long.”

questions.prompt: Which mindset matches the Appearance Standard?
options: Groom properly only when expecting many clients or when management is present.
If the therapist is available to attend to a client, the therapist should be client-ready. Appearance is part of the client’s experience.
Hygiene can wait until after the first session.
Colleagues are responsible for reminding you every day.

title: SECTION B — UNIFORM, HAIR AND HYGIENE

questions.prompt: The approved uniform is stained and smells of sweat, but the therapist has a client waiting. What should they do?
options: Attend the client anyway because the massage will hide it.
Cover the smell with extra perfume and proceed.
Change into a clean, fresh, properly worn uniform before receiving the client, and inspect the uniform before the first client.
Tell the client that uniforms do not matter.

questions.prompt: Long hair keeps falling onto the client and into the oil during massage. What is the issue?
options: Nothing. Hair is always allowed on the client.
Hair should be clean, neat, controlled, and secured so it does not fall on the client, into oil, or require constant touching.
The client should hold the therapist’s hair.
Only short hair is allowed at Zura Spa.

questions.prompt: A therapist did not bathe and uses heavy body spray to cover body odour. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing. Fragrance replaces bathing.
Fragrance supports cleanliness. It does not replace cleanliness. The therapist should not rely on perfume or body spray to cover poor hygiene.
Body spray is banned even after bathing.
Clients prefer strong fragrance over freshness.

questions.prompt: A therapist becomes excessively sweaty mid-shift and still has another client. What is the responsible action?
options: Attend the next client immediately without freshening up.
Freshen up as needed, including changing clothing if it has absorbed excessive sweat, then continue.
Ask the client to ignore the smell.
Spray more perfume and skip deodorant.

title: SECTION C — BREATH, HANDS, ACCESSORIES AND FOOTWEAR

questions.prompt: Why is fresh breath part of the Appearance Standard?
options: Because therapists never speak to clients.
Because the therapist may communicate at close range, so breath is part of appearance and hygiene.
Because chewing gum throughout the massage is required.
Because mouthwash replaces brushing forever.

questions.prompt: A therapist chews gum visibly throughout a professional massage session. What should guide them instead?
options: Chewing gum should not become distracting. The therapist should never be chewing gum visibly throughout a professional massage session.
Gum is the best way to show friendliness.
Gum is required after every sentence to the client.
The client should also chew gum.

questions.prompt: Before massage, the therapist should personally ask: “Are my hands safe and comfortable for this client’s skin?” What does that include?
options: Hands that are dirty as long as oil is applied.
Hands that are clean, maintained, free from visible dirt and offensive odour, and nails that are clean, short enough, smooth, and free from sharp or broken edges.
Excessively long nails to look fashionable.
Jewelry that scratches, as long as it is gold.

questions.prompt: Which accessories should be removed before massage?
options: None. Accessories always improve the service.
Large bracelets, noisy jewelry, sharp rings, items that can scratch, items that interfere with movement, and excessive accessories that distract from a professional appearance.
Only watches belonging to clients.
All clothing, including the uniform.

questions.prompt: A therapist wears dirty, noisy shoes that slap on the treatment-room floor. Why is this a problem?
options: Footwear has no standard.
Footwear should be clean, suitable, safe, quiet enough not to disturb relaxation, and free from offensive odour. Noisy footwear disrupts a relaxing environment.
Louder shoes help clients stay awake.
Dirty shoes show the therapist has been working hard.

title: SECTION D — CHECKS, TEAM AND CORRECTION

questions.prompt: Before becoming available for clients, what should every therapist do?
options: Skip checks if they feel busy.
Conduct a brief personal appearance check: uniform, hair, hygiene, breath, hands and nails, accessories, footwear, then a final mirror check.
Ask a colleague to get dressed for them.
Fix hair and clothing in front of the waiting client.

questions.prompt: What is the final mirror-check question?
options: “Will management see me today?”
“If I were the client meeting this therapist for the first time, would this appearance give me confidence?” If no, correct the issue before attending to the client.
“Do I look more attractive than my colleague?”
“Can I start even if I am not ready?”

questions.prompt: A colleague has a stain they may not have noticed. What is the better team response?
options: Allow them to attend the client unaware, then gossip later.
Tell them privately and respectfully so they can correct it before the client is affected. Every therapist is still primarily responsible for their own appearance.
Humiliate them in the corridor.
Repeatedly take over their basic grooming every day as your job.

questions.prompt: During 4-hands massage, one therapist has poor hygiene. Why does this matter to the other therapist?
options: It does not. Only one therapist is judged.
Both therapists represent the service together. The client’s dissatisfaction may affect both, so one person’s lack of preparation can embarrass the co-therapist.
The professional therapist should copy the poor standard.
4-hands massage has no appearance standard.

questions.prompt: A supervisor says, “Your uniform has become stained. Please change before taking another client.” What is the professional response?
options: Respond defensively and attend the client anyway.
Accept correction immediately and practically. An accidental stain plus immediate correction is a normal workplace issue.
Ignore it because massage skill compensates for poor hygiene.
Argue that appearance is a personal choice once you are on shift.

title: SECTION E — ACCOUNTABILITY AND THE STANDARD

questions.prompt: When does an appearance issue become more than an accident?
options: The first time a uniform wrinkles slightly.
When the same appearance or hygiene problem continues after repeated correction — it becomes a failure to maintain the professional standard.
Never. Appearance is always optional.
Only if a client writes a review.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the Zura Spa Appearance Standard?
options: SKIP CHECKS → COVER WITH PERFUME → ATTEND ANYWAY
CLEAN → CHECK → GROOM → FRESHEN → DRESS → PRESENT → MAINTAIN
LOOK ATTRACTIVE → IGNORE HYGIENE → HOPE THE CLIENT DOES NOT NOTICE
GROOM ONLY WHEN MANAGEMENT IS PRESENT
